A rejoinder is a reply — but not just any reply. It is a sharp, quick, pointed response that someone gives in the middle of an argument, debate, or disagreement. It usually comes as a direct answer to what the other person just said, and it often has a clever, witty, or cutting edge to it.

Think of it as a comeback with brains.

The English language has many words for "reply" — answer, response, retort, rebuttal — so why does rejoinder exist? Because it captures something specific that those other words don't fully capture.

A rejoinder is special for two reasons:

1. It is a reply to a reply.
A rejoinder doesn't just happen at the start of a conversation. It happens mid-exchange, after the back-and-forth has already begun. Someone says something → you respond → they fire back → your next response to their counter-response is a rejoinder. It lives in the thick of an ongoing verbal clash.

2. It is quick and pointed.
A rejoinder is not a slow, thoughtful letter you write after sleeping on it. It is immediate and direct. It hits the exact point the other person raised, and it hits it hard — often with wit or sharpness.

Imagine two people arguing about whether a movie was good:

Person A: "That film was a masterpiece."
Person B: "Masterpiece? It was two hours of nothing happening."
Person A: "Nothing happening? You clearly weren't paying attention."

Person A's last line — "You clearly weren't paying attention" — is a rejoinder. It directly addresses Person B's specific criticism and fires back in a sharp, immediate way.

A rejoinder typically carries one of these flavors:

  • Witty — clever and maybe a little playful
  • Sharp — cutting, straight to the point
  • Dismissive — swatting away the other person's argument
  • Confident — spoken with the assurance of someone who believes they've just won the point

It is rarely soft, polite, or gentle. A timid, meek reply is almost never called a rejoinder. The word implies some bite.

In formal law — particularly in older legal systems — rejoinder has a precise technical meaning. In a court case, when both sides submit written arguments, the sequence goes like this:

  • The plaintiff (the person suing) makes their claim.
  • The defendant responds to that claim.
  • The plaintiff then replies to the defendant's response.
  • The defendant then responds to that reply — and this specific response is called a rejoinder.

So even in law, the logic is the same: it is a reply to a reply, arriving at a specific stage of the exchange. This usage is largely historical and rare in modern courtrooms, but you may encounter it in older legal texts or literature.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are close relatives of rejoinder, but each has its own personality:

Retort — Also a sharp reply, but retort often feels more aggressive or angry, like someone snapping back in frustration. A rejoinder can be sharp and cool-headed.

Riposte — A quick, clever comeback. Very similar to rejoinder, but riposte (borrowed from fencing) puts more emphasis on the speed and elegance of the reply.

Rebuttal — A response that focuses on disproving an argument with logic or evidence. A rebuttal is more formal and systematic; a rejoinder is sharper and more conversational.

Comeback — The everyday, informal version. A rejoinder is essentially a sophisticated, formal way of saying "comeback."

Answer / Response / Reply — These are neutral, all-purpose words. A rejoinder is a specific kind of reply — one with sharpness and direction in the middle of an argument.

• His speech was interrupted several times, but he had a cool rejoinder ready for every heckler.
  • She expected him to apologize, but instead he offered a stinging rejoinder that left her speechless.
  • The debate was lively, with each candidate's rejoinder sharper than the last.
  • "Is that your best argument?" she asked. His rejoinder was swift: "No, I'm saving that for when you say something worth answering properly."
When You Would Use This Word

You would use rejoinder when you want to describe a reply that:

  • Happens in the middle of an argument, debate, or heated exchange
  • Is directed precisely at what the other person just said
  • Has a quality of being sharp, smart, or pointed
  • Suggests the speaker was quick on their feet

It is a word more common in formal writing, literary prose, journalism, and intellectual discussion than in casual everyday speech. If you use it in your writing, it will add a sense of sophistication and precision to your description of a conversation.
A rejoinder is a sharp, quick, pointed reply made in the middle of an argument or debate — specifically as a direct response to what the other person just said.
